related.en: the triumphant shout after a prank

note: April Fools' Day is «Дан шале». A successful prank ends with a triumphant «Априли-ли-ли!»
title: April Fools' Day

note:
In songs and subtitles Serbian is often typed in «bald Latin», without š, ž, č, ć. Then different words merge:
• sisati (си̏сати) - to suck, but šišati (ши́шати) - to cut hair
• koza (ко̀за) - goat, but koža (ко̏жа) - skin

So for study it is better to use texts in Cyrillic or in full Latin.
title: Latin without diacritics changes the meaning

related.en: duplex (a house for two families; a two-story apartment)
apartment with its own exit to the yard
house for two or three families

note:
A private family house is often built with several floors: the head of the family plans ahead for where his son will bring his wife.

Other types:
• гарсо̀њера - a studio apartment
• ду̏плекс - a house for two families with a shared wall, or a two-story apartment
• дворѝшни ста̑н - an apartment with an exit to the yard, more often an illegal one
• ку̏ћа на̏пола - a house for two or three families
title: Types of housing in Serbia

related.en: Serbian New Year (the Old New Year, January 13)
family celebration of the patron saint (slava)

note:
New Year is not the main family holiday in Serbia. It is celebrated four times:
1. On the daytime of December 31 young people go out to cafes for a «дне̏вна жу̑рка».
2. At night - parties in restaurants and squares with live music (жи̏ва сви̑рка).
3. On the evening of January 1 - the «репрѝза» in bars.
4. January 13 - Ср̏пска Но̑ва го̏дина (by the Old Style calendar), often even louder.

The main family holidays are Сла̏ва, Бо̀жић and У̏скрс.
title: Serbs celebrate New Year four times

note:
What Serbs like:
• ра̀кија - fruit brandy, offered to guests
• ка̀фа, Turkish style
• бу̀рек with yogurt as a snack
• ро̀штӣљ for any celebration
• Plazma biscuits as the taste of childhood
• comfortable sportswear

The music is наро̀дњаци and ту̏рбо-фо̑лк, especially at weddings.
title: The Serbian cultural code: food and habits

note:
Serbian schoolchildren chose пра̏скозо̄рје as the most beautiful word: the twilight before dawn, a symbol of hope and a new beginning.

Other favorites include ши̏шмиш, си̏јалица, шаргаре́па, кикирѝки, пара̀дајз, бомбо̀њера, ужѝвајте.

An interesting word is ра̀збибрига - any pastime, like a crossword.
title: The most beautiful Serbian word

note:
For English speakers the trickiest letter is «Ј» (J in Latin): it is read like English «y» in «yes», not like «j» in «jam». For example Јо̀ван (Yovan), Ја̀смӣн (Yasmin), Јо̀рдан (Yordan).

Rules:
• do not mix Latin and Cyrillic in one word
• Љ and њ in Latin are Lj and Nj
• Đ is written exactly so, not «Dj»: Doviđenja (довиђе́ња), not Dovidjenja
• the word је is read «ye», as in «yes»
title: The letter J is the trickiest

note:
Рамо̀нда is a Balkan flower that looks like a violet. It revives after almost completely drying out, so it is a symbol of rebirth. Serbia's song at Eurovision 2024 was named after it.

Да̀ница is the Serbian name of Venus, the morning star, the «herald of the day». It is also a female name and a synonym of rare beauty.
title: Ramonda and the star Danica

note:
In a readers' poll the least pleasant-sounding Serbian word was «ко̏пиле» (a child born out of wedlock).

Also on the list:
• ке̏ва - colloquial for mother
• ћа̏ле - colloquial for father
• пѝнђур, по̀дбрадак, гно̑ј

Many of these words are about children and parents, which shows how much Serbs value family.
title: The least beautiful Serbian words

note:
Serbs especially love quince (ду̏ња): it is kept on top of the wardrobe for its scent, rakija is made from it, poems are written about it, and Ду̏ња is a girl's name.

Ма̀лина matters too: Serbia is a major exporter of raspberries, and Ма̀лина is a female name.
title: Quince, the favorite fruit of Serbs

note:
In Nj and Lj the letter j is not a separate «y» sound: each pair is one soft consonant, with no pause after it.

Examples:
• љу̀ља̄шка - roughly «lyoo-lya-shka», with a soft «ly» as in «million»
• њу̏шка - roughly «nyoo-shka», with «ny» as in «canyon»

Respellings are always approximate, so it is better to listen to the audio.
title: Lj and Nj are single sounds

related.en: a stew cooked in a cauldron

note:
Labor Day (Пр̀вӣ ма̏ј, Пра̑знӣк ра̑да): May 1 and 2 are days off.

Adults go to a spa town, to other countries, or to a barbecue (ро̀штӣљ, ко̏тлић).

Young people claim spots in the forest in advance by tying ribbons to the trees, and live in tents for up to three days with loud music.
title: May Day: barbecue and tents

note:
Parents call their children «Си̑не!» (a son or a daughter) and «Ћеро!» (a daughter only).

In congratulations and invitations the woman's name comes first.

To speak about a person's qualities, «о̏соба» is better, because «чо̏век» often means «man».
title: Сине! and Ћеро! - forms of address to children

note:
Serbs write and pronounce English names with «в» (v) in place of W:
• Ро̑н Ви̏зли, Вѝлијам Ше̏кспир, Ви̏нстон Че̏рчил
• Во̑лт Ди̏зни, Бру̑с Ви̏лис, Е̏ма Во̏тсон

The same in words: вѝкенд, Ви̏мблдон, Во̑л стри̑т.

Cartoon characters are often adapted: the Flintstones are По̀родица Кре̏менко, Huey, Dewey and Louie are Ра́ја, Га̏ја и Вла̏ја.
title: English W becomes «В» in Serbian

note:
In Serbia relatives and close friends often drop in without calling. This is not rude: advance notice makes the hosts fuss, while a sudden visit is simply a reason to chat.

If guests did warn you a week ahead, they most likely expect a proper feast.
title: Guests without warning

skip: Russian words that have no exact Serbian equivalent; makes sense only for a Russian speaker

note:
There is no single word for it. People say:
• жу̑рка са колѐгама
• корпора̀тивна жу̑рка
• пра̏знична жу̑рка на по̏слу
• корпора̀тивна про̏слава
• the loanword ти̏мбилдинг - barbecue, bowling, paintball, a bar

A New Year company party is «новогодишња прослава са колегама».
title: How to say «company party» in Serbian

related.en: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

note:
«Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs» in Serbian is «Снежана и седам патуљака». Пату́љак means both a dwarf and a little person.

The dwarfs' names are made from verbs and adjectives:
• Уча (from у̀чити) - the smart one
• Љутко (from љу́тити се) - Grumpy
• Сре̏ћко (from сре̏ћан) - Happy
• Поспа́нко (from по̏спа̄н) - Sleepy
• Стидљивко (from сти́дети се) - Bashful
• Кијавко (from ки́јати) - Sneezy
• Тупко (from ту̑п) - Dopey: not an insult but an affectionate «silly»
title: Names of the seven dwarfs in Serbian

note:
People in Novi Sad call a guy «гари» - roughly like «dude» or «buddy».

A local pride is the «Ѝндекс» sandwich, invented in Novi Sad.

Humorous videos about the city feature a кафа̀на, a band of тамбу̀раши (tamburitza players) and the Мѝшелук district, where fans of fast driving gather.
title: Novi Sad slang: «гари» and «Индекс»

note:
In Serbia persimmons are often sold as «јапа̀нска ја̏бука» (literally «Japanese apple»), with «каки» in brackets on the price tag.

A seller asking «Колѝко ка̀ки?» wants to know how many fruits you want, but parents of small children hear «how much does he poop?» (какити is baby talk for to poop).

A case where Serbian is funny quite literally.
title: The persimmon «каки» and a funny coincidence

related.en: pljeskavica (a large patty of minced meat)

note:
The Serbian «ру̏ска сала́та» is basically Olivier salad, with some differences:
• the peas are boiled, not canned
• the mayonnaise is Serbian, with a hint of mustard, and a lot of it goes in

This salad is on the table at every celebration, and it is even put into a пљѐскавица.

In other European countries the same salad is called Russian, French or beef salad.
title: «Руска салата» on the Serbian table

related.en: at the top of one's voice

note:
Serbian kindergartens teach New Year songs about Father Frost (Де̏да Мра̑з): «Са̏нке Де̏да Мра̏за» and «Звончићи» (the Serbian version of Jingle Bells).

The lyrics include па̀хуља, са̏нке, и̏рва̄с, окле́вати and the phrase на са̏в гла̑с.
title: New Year songs for children

related.en: the custom of searching for gifts in straw
oak branch for the Christmas Eve fire

note:
On Serbian Christmas Eve (Ба̑дњи да̑н, January 6) straw (сла̏ма) is brought into the house, and coins, tangerines and sweets are hidden in it.

Children look for the gifts and peep «пи̏јӯ-пи̏јӯ» like chicks, hence the name «пи̏јука̄ње».

The custom is relaxed and has many variants: at church, at home, or by a fire with oak branches, the «ба̏дња̄к».
title: «Пијукање» on Christmas Eve

note:
On Serbian signs a ban or a warning is usually expressed with a verb in the imperative:
• «Не гази траву» - keep off the grass
• «Не дирај» - do not touch
• «Не бацај ђубре» - do not litter
• «Пази» - careful, watch out
• «Чувај се пса» - beware of the dog

On doors: «Вуци» - pull, «Гурај» - push.

A «Па̏ӯк» on a parking sign means a tow truck.
title: Inscriptions and warnings on signs

related.en: to dance on the spot, to bounce in place

note:
At a concert with seats, Serbs more often stand up and dance right by their seats, without going out into the aisle. This bouncing in one place is called «ђу̏скање».

Even in clubs there is no separate dance floor: guests stand by their sofas and tall round tables.

Lively fun is a sign of respect for the hosts, and it is rather the one who sits that gets judged.
title: How Serbs dance at concerts

related.en: decorating the guests at a wedding

note:
The first thing that awaits a guest at a wedding restaurant is ки̏ће̄ње (literally «decorating»).

At the entrance stand two baskets with decorations, for men and for women. The guest is given a bracelet or a pin for the chest and puts money into another basket in return - usually a few hundred or a couple of thousand dinars.
title: «Кићење» at a wedding

note:
On the menu look for «то̏пла̄ прѐдјела» (hot appetizers): they serve grilled Miroč cheese from Mount Miroč in Eastern Serbia. It squeaks on the teeth, hence the folk name «шкри̏павац».

A sweet classic is ке̏сте̄н-пи̏ре, a dessert of chestnut puree with sugar, rum and milk, topped with whipped cream.

In bakeries get a crunchy пѐреца.
title: Serbian treats: Miroč cheese and chestnut puree

note:
The word цр̑н has many shades in Serbian:
• црно вино - red wine
• цр̑нӣ лу̏к - a common cooking onion
• поцр̀нети - to get a tan
• цр̑нӣ да̑ни - hard times
• црне паре - tainted money

In the expression «цр̑нӣ ђа̏во̄» it makes a curse stronger.

A literal translation is often wrong.
title: «Црн» is not only «black»

note:
Numbers:
• police (полѝција) - 192
• fire service - 193
• ambulance - 194
• roadside assistance (А̏МСС) - 1987

Useful words: хи̏тно је, по̏жа̄р, у по̏мо̄ћ, па̏зите, ѝзгубљен сам.
title: Emergency numbers in Serbia

skip: False friends with Russian words (реч, рок, част, фамилија...); makes sense only for a Russian speaker

note:
Many countries are named with the feminine form of an adjective: Фра̀нцӯска̄, Нѐмачка̄, Ма̏ђарска̄, Ѐнгле̄ска̄, Шве̏дска̄ (literally «the French (land)», «the German (land)» and so on).

Some names are not what you would expect:
• Ма̏ђарска̄ - Hungary
• Нѐмачка̄ - Germany
• Уједѝњено Кра́љевство - the United Kingdom
• СА̑Д - the USA
title: Country names in Serbian

related.en: The fish is gnawing at the fish's tail

related.sr: Чѐтири чавчѝћа на чу̏нчићу чу́че̄ћи ци̏јучу
related.en: Four little jackdaws crouching on a little boat are chirping
Petar is weaving a fence for Petar

note:
A classic tongue twister: «Риба риби гризе реп».

To practice the sounds «ћ», «ч» and «ц»: «Четири чавчића на чунчићу чучећи цијучу». For «р» and «ј», «Петар Петру плете плот» is good.
title: Serbian tongue twisters

skip: False friends with Russian words on с- and т-; makes sense only for a Russian speaker

note:
For doors: «Вуци» - pull, «Гурај» - push.

Warnings: «Не дирај», «Не гази траву», «Не бацај ђубре», «Тишѝна».

On fences: «Чувај се пса». In a parking area: «Забрањено паркирање».

Most inscriptions use the imperative in the informal «ти» form.
title: Signs in the street and in the building

note:
«Љ» and «њ» are ligatures made of «л» and «н» with a soft sign. The letter «џ» came from Romanian Cyrillic.

These letters exist only in the Serbian alphabet (and some related ones): they stand for sounds that are spelled lj (like «lli» in «million»), nj (like «ny» in «canyon») and dž (like «j» in «jam») in Latin.

Examples: љу́бав, њѐгов, џе̏п.
title: Special letters of Serbian Cyrillic

note:
The name of a place is often made from the goods plus the suffix -ара: мѐсара, пѝљара, књѝжара, пѐкара. There is also мѐња̄чница.

Other signs:
• печѐњара - a place selling roast meat
• посластѝчарница - a pastry shop
• амбула̀нта - a health clinic
• вулканѝзер - a tire repair shop
• ро̏бна ку̏ћа - a department store
• бензѝнска пу̑мпа - a gas station
title: What shops and places are called on signs

skip: False friends with Russian words on у-, ј-, к-; makes sense only for a Russian speaker
Only a warning not to confuse привреда with the Russian «привередливый»; makes sense only for a Russian speaker

note:
English has only «you», but Serbian distinguishes the informal «ти» from the formal «ви̑». Serbs switch to «ти» quickly: young people, sellers and waiters often say «ти» right away.

If the formal form bothers you, you can say «немој да ми персираш». Перси́рати means to address someone with «ви».

Politeness is shown by tone and by words like мо̏лим and изво̀лите.
title: Serbs quickly switch to «ти»

note:
Serbian has two equal alphabets: Cyrillic (ћирѝлица) and Latin (латѝница). Cyrillic is the official script of the state, but signs, packaging and social media often use Latin.

Almost every Serb reads both fluently. The correspondence is one to one: љ - lj, њ - nj, џ - dž.
title: Two alphabets: Cyrillic and Latin

note:
In everyday speech:
• руска салата - Russian salad (Olivier)
• руска зима - very severe cold
• ру̏скӣ фи̏лм - a hard, tragic story

These are humorous images, not political statements.
title: What «руски» means in Serbian expressions

note:
Жу́па is a Slavic word for a settled territory among hills and valleys. Жу̀пан is the medieval title of a regional ruler, and вѐликӣ жу̀пан is the supreme prince.

In Croatia and Hungary a жупа̀нија is an administrative unit; in Serbia the closest modern equivalent is the сре̑з.

The word appears in place names: Жу́па Александро̀вачка, Среда̀чка жу́па.
title: «Жупа» is a historical region

note:
More than five centuries next to the Ottoman Empire left many Turkish loanwords:
• household: јо̀рган, ћѝлим, ме̏рдевине, со̀ка̄к, ћорсо̀ка̄к
• food: са̀рма, бу̀рек, бакла̀ва, ће̏вап
• people and relations: ко̀мшија, комшѝлук, ду̏шманин, о̀рта̄к

They sound lively and colloquial.
title: Turkish words in Serbian

note:
In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić simplified Serbian Cyrillic:
• he kept 24 of the old letters
• he added «ј», «љ», «њ», «ћ», «ђ», «џ»
• he dropped the superfluous ones (such as «ѣ»)

The principle: write as you hear, read as it is written. This brought the written language closer to the speech of the people.
title: Vuk Karadžić's reform

related.en: to be stubborn out of spite

related.sr: о̑н не̏ће да пи̑ше̄ латѝницом, о̑н је ср̀бе̄нда
related.en: he refuses to write in Latin script, he is a србенда

note:
Ѝна̄т is stubbornness out of spite, even to one's own harm. Of a person one may say «у ње̏му је ѝна̄т» (he has inat in him).

The humorous «ср̀бе̄нда» means a super-patriot: «он неће да пише латиницом, он је србенда» (he won't write in Latin script, he is a србенда).
title: «Српски инат» - Serbian spite and stubbornness

note:
It is customary to bring a gift when visiting Serbs:
• for the hostess (дома̀ћица) - flowers or sweets
• for the host (дома̀ћин) - a bottle of rakija (ра̀кија) or wine
• for children - chocolate

The hosts will first protest that you should not have - answer «Ма̏ ка̀квӣ, нѝје то̑ ни̏шта».

You are expected to eat a lot: «Је̏ди, ни̏шта не је̏де̄ш!»

Offering to help in the kitchen is good manners. It is better to stay away from politics.
title: Visiting Serbs

note:
The most typical gift is coffee (ка̀фа), about 200 grams: 100 is too little, more looks like showing off.

What to give to whom:
• often - chocolate and a бомбо̀њера
• to women - flowers
• to men - a bottle of rakija or wine
• to children - sweets or fruit
• to the elderly - coffee and ра́тлук
title: What is customary to give as a gift in Serbia

note:
Домаћа кафа is Turkish coffee made in a džezva, the most common order.

Young people often drink нес кафа (instant coffee), топли нес or хладни нес, and espresso:
• кра̀ткӣ - short
• ду̏плӣ - double
• продужени - with added water
• еспресо са млеком - espresso with milk

Simply saying «Једну кафу, молим» or «Ја ћу домаћу» is perfectly normal.
title: How to order coffee in Serbia

note:
The most common is шљи̏вовица, made from plums.

Other kinds:
• комо̀вица - from grape pomace, also drunk as a medicine
• лозова̀ча - straight from grapes, popular in Montenegro
• кајсијѐвача - from apricots
• дуњева̀ча - from quince
• ви̏љамовка - from pears
• трава̀рица - plum brandy with herbs
• клеко̀вача - with juniper

Among the liqueurs: медо̀вача, орахова̀ча, вишњѐвача.
title: Kinds of rakija

note:
Serbia distinguishes three kinds of beef:
• тѐлетина - veal, a calf under a year old, light tender meat
• јунѐтина - young cattle of 12-24 months, redder meat
• го̀ведина - from cattle older than two years, dark red, with richer fat
title: Veal, young beef and beef: телетина, јунетина, говедина

note:
For Serbs summer begins on the day of the summer solstice (about June 21) and lasts until the September equinox. Spring begins around March 20.

Congratulating someone on the first day of summer on June 1 would seem odd.

Ле̏то is the season of vacations and school holidays, but же̏га wears out pensioners.
title: Summer by the calendar: when it starts

note:
Wedding customs:
• in front of the procession walks the барја̀кта̄р with a flag
• the groom shoots at an apple on a branch at the bride's house
• ку̑м and ку́ма are the witnesses, often later the godparents
• after the church the кум throws coins to the crowd
• at the feast the bride's shoe is «stolen» and returned for a ransom
• before the church the bride lifts a baby for the sake of future children
title: The Serbian wedding: traditions

note:
Бре̏ strengthens a phrase and adds emotion: surprise, irritation, joy. It is not a swear word and not an exact equivalent of «dude» or «damn». It suits friends and family, but not your boss.

Examples:
• «Ма бежи, бре!» - Oh, come off it!
• «Шта̏ је, бре̏, о̀во̄?» - What on earth is this?

The word exists in Greek and Turkish too.
title: «Бре» - the universal particle

skip: False friends with Russian words; makes sense only for a Russian speaker

related.en: You are missing one more paper

note:
Ша̀лтерка is a humorous word for a female clerk at a counter (ша̀лтер) who handles bureaucratic matters.

The meme: whatever you bring, she will say «Фали ти један папир» (you are missing one more paper), abbreviated FT1P.
title: «Шалтерка» and FT1P

note:
The base is the grill (ро̀штӣљ): a пљѐскавица (a large patty, often stuffed with cheese and ham) and ћева̀пи.

You choose the toppings yourself, usually at no extra charge: ку̀пус сала́та, кра̏ставац, пара̀дајз, ка̀јмак, у̏рнебе̄с.

You can say «Све̏ по̀мало» (a bit of everything). To take it away: «за по̀нети».
title: Serbian fast food

note:
Serbian superstitions:
• «Жи́вели» is not said with water or juice - it brings trouble
• you must not whistle in the house, you will attract mice
• a bag is not put on the floor: you will lose money
• bread must not be put upside down
• an itchy right palm means spending, the left one means money
• when clinking glasses, you look the person in the eye
title: Serbian superstitions

note:
Some sounds differ from English:
• duck - ква-ква
• frog - кре-кре
• piglet - гро-гро or скви-скви
• hen - ко-ко-да
• mouse - циу-циу
• pigeon - гу-гу-гу

Close to English: ав-ав (woof), мјау (meow), му-му (moo).

A cat is called with «мац-мац», like English «kitty-kitty».
title: Animal sounds in Serbian

related.en: like a Russian vehicle (said of something that eats up a lot of money)

note:
More «руски» in Serbian jokes:
• ру̏скӣ те̏нк - a very big person
• руски лекари - mysterious experts everyone talks about
• ру̏скӣ тра̏ктор - something that never breaks
• ру̏скӣ во̀лети - to love unconditionally
• ко руско возило - to spend a lot of money
title: More «руски» in Serbian jokes
